A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' instrumental-variable approach to selective labels. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support comparison despite the changed title and expanded multiclass scope.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D report original semi-synthetic FICO experiments, including accuracy distributions across selection-bias and missingness settings.

after.justification: Section 7 reports original synthetic three-class experiments and semi-synthetic binary FICO experiments, illustrated in Figures 2–7.

M1.justification: v1's binary weighted classification procedure becomes a multiclass UCL algorithm with class-specific costs, vector-valued scores, a softmax surrogate objective, and argmax prediction. The point/partial identification modes and cross-fitting remain, but the multiclass procedure is a substantive extension rather than a rename.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates binary classification on semi-synthetic FICO data. v3 retains that task and adds a fully synthetic three-class task with Gaussian observed and unobserved features, substantially expanding the evaluated population and prediction requirements.

E2.justification: SelectedSample(IPW) is added to the FICO comparison alongside the existing selected-sample and full-sample references. It also participates in the new synthetic study. The five underlying FICO classifiers remain AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and SVM.

E3.justification: The new synthetic evaluation introduces 10,000 observations, five observed and five unobserved features, five decision-makers, and a neural-network classifier with histogram-gradient-boosting nuisance estimation. The retained FICO evaluation still uses a 70:30 split, five-fold cross-fitting, and five-fold hyperparameter cross-validation; these are not new settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds separate sensitivity sweeps over unobserved-variable effects on outcomes and selection, with alpha_Y and alpha_D each taking 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7 under NUCEM and UC models. Conversely, v1 Appendix D's increased-missingness tests at beta=0.5 and 0.25 are removed.

E5.justification: v3 specifies 100 repetitions for the new synthetic study, while the retained FICO study still uses 50. Both versions display repeated-run distributions using boxplots; no new confidence-interval, significance-testing, or seed-reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: The FICO plots contain changed results: for example, selected-sample Logistic Regression at alpha=0.9 under Model 1/NUCEM has a plotted median accuracy of approximately 0.63 in v1 versus 0.61 in v3. v3 also adds IPW and multiclass results, including PointLearning underperforming selected-sample baselines in several synthetic settings, and removes the beta=0.5/0.25 results.

T1.justification: v3 adds an overlap assumption, multiclass identification and simplex-constrained risk formulations, a converse for covariance-ratio identification, and new tightness, calibration, and decision-maker-leniency results. Appendix D replaces v1's binary bound containing an approximation term with a K-dependent best-in-class guarantee. These are substantive mathematical changes, beyond relocating proofs.

C1.justification: The contribution expands from binary weighted learning to multiclass cost-sensitive learning. v3's conclusion also claims necessary and sufficient identification conditions, whereas v1 presents sufficient conditions. The central claim of robust learning under both point and partial identification remains.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes the effects of hidden variables on predictability and selection bias, explains why IPW cannot remove hidden-variable bias, and discusses PointLearning's failures at weaker confounding. Appendix B.4 adds interpretations connecting decision-maker heterogeneity and leniency to bound tightness. The explanation that covariance-ratio estimation makes PointLearning unstable already appears in v1.

D1.justification: v3 supplies explicit synthetic generation coefficients in Equation (7.1), PyTorch/softmax implementation guidance, histogram-gradient-boosting details for the new study, and a FICO data-access URL. The existing FICO processing and fitting information is largely retained; detailed neural-network architecture and training budgets remain unspecified.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands its treatment of counterfactual evaluation, multicategory treatment-rule learning, and minimax policy learning, with added citations such as Coston et al. and Zhang et al. The relationship to Rambachan et al. (2022) changes from their bounds recovering this work's bounds to claiming this work's bounds are slightly tighter.

P1.justification: The title and substantial portions of the narrative are rewritten. v3 introduces a Main Contributions subsection, makes Related Work a separate section, separates exact and partial identification into full sections, and reorganizes the appendices while moving generalization analysis out of the main text.

P2.justification: The combined FICO display is replaced by separate NUCEM and UC plots with changed method ordering, legends, axes, and an IPW group. Two nine-panel synthetic figures are added, and the missingness-sensitivity figures disappear. v3 also duplicates identical FICO plots as Figures 2/6 and 3/7; these are repeated displays, not additional experiments.

improvement.justification: The multiclass extension, synthetic sensitivity study, and IPW comparison provide substantial new substance and evidence. However, v3 removes the increased-missingness tests and introduces theoretical reliability concerns: Equation (D.5)'s best-in-class guarantee is not justified by Theorem 5's unrestricted calibration bound, and Theorem 7's stringent-decision-maker upper-bound claim conflicts with Theorem 3's formula under ordered decision rules. These gains and unresolved mathematical problems prevent a confident net quality judgment.
